Homework 3

Model Building, Cross-Validation, and Shrinkage

Author

Rex Green

Data and Goal

Measuring body fat accurately can require underwater weighing. Researchers collected age, weight, height, and neck, chest, and abdomen circumference measurements for 252 men. The response brozek is body-fat percentage estimated using underwater weighing. Your goal is to build a simpler model that predicts brozek from the noninvasive measurements.

The file BodyFat.txt is in the Data/ folder supplied with this module. Keep the provided folder structure intact so the path ../Data/BodyFat.txt works from this homework file.

Multicollinearity

4. Diagnose multicollinearity

Fit brozek ~ . on bodyfat and call it bodyfat_full_mod. Report all VIFs, the maximum VIF, and the mean VIF. Decide whether multicollinearity is a meaningful problem and identify the predictors most responsible. Treat the usual thresholds as rules of thumb, not automatic pass/fail cutoffs.

bodyfat_full_mod <- lm(brozek ~ . , data = bodyfat)
vif(bodyfat_full_mod) |> round(4)
    age  weight  height    neck   chest   abdom 
 1.5408 19.8957  2.6696  3.1246  9.0382  9.7005 
max(vif(bodyfat_full_mod))
[1] 19.89574
mean(vif(bodyfat_full_mod))
[1] 7.661578

The maximum VIF is 19.90, for the weight coefficient. The other VIFs are 9.70 for abdomen, 9.03 for chest, 3.12 for neck, 2.66 for heigh, and 1.54 for age, giving a mean VIF is 7.66.
I think that multicollinearity is a meaningful problem in this case. The most responsible predictors are weight, abdomen, and chest. This makes sense because extra weight tends to collect near the gut, so the weight, chest, and abdomen are associated with both each other and with higher brozek scores.

5. Connect VIF to coefficient uncertainty

For the predictor with the largest VIF:

  1. Fit the auxiliary regression of that predictor on all the other predictors.
  2. Use its auxiliary Rj2 to calculate VIFj=1/(1−Rj2) by hand.
  3. Calculate VIFj and interpret that value as a standard-error inflation factor.
weight_regression <- lm(weight ~ . - brozek, data = bodyfat)
summary(weight_regression)

6. Explain the apparent contradiction

A model can have a strong overall R2 and useful fitted values while its individual coefficients are unstable because of multicollinearity. Explain why these statements can both be true. Your explanation should use the idea of how much independent information the data contain about each predictor after holding the others fixed.

These statements are both be true because when we compute the overall R2 and the fitted values for the model we choose, those fitted values are interpreted as “holding all other predictors constant”. This becomes a problem in situations where it is difficult to hold other predictors constant (one example would be height and wingspan for basketball players - taller players tend to have larger wingspans). So if we hold height fixed and vary wingspan, the model will tell us that players with larger wingspan tend to be better players, ignoring the fact that height also helps a lot. The data leaves out critical information that helps us to make a decision based on everything we know.

8. Interpret AIC, BIC, algorithms, and metrics

Answer each part in complete sentences.

  1. Did AIC and BIC select the same model? Explain why they are not required to agree.
  2. In the preceding analysis, what was the search algorithm, and what were the two selection metrics?
  3. Which metric usually penalizes additional predictors more strongly when n is reasonably large, and what consequence does that tend to have for model size?
  1. AIC and BIC did not select the same model because they are two different measures that prioritize different aspects. This is acceptable because the two criteria exist to serve different purposes - AIC favors larger models that could have more predictive signals, while BIC favors more interpretable and simpler models.
  2. In the predicing analysis, the search algorithm was best-subsets selection, and the two selection metrics were AIC and BIC.
  3. The metric that usually penalizes additional predictors more strongly is BIC. This tend to shrink model size, which improves interpretability but can make reliable prediction more difficult.

9. Explain a limitation of forward selection

Suppose x1 is the best one-predictor model, but {x2,x3} is the best two-predictor model according to AIC. Explain why forward selection can fail to reach {x2,x3} even though best subsets can find it. Identify the exact greedy decision that causes the problem.

Forward selection can fail to reach {x2,x3} because it cannot remove a predictor once it added. The decision to cause the problem is the decision to add x1 to the model without checking any other combinations of variables.

11. Explain the bias-variance tradeoff and choose a method

Answer each part in complete sentences.

  1. Ridge and LASSO deliberately bias coefficient estimates. Explain how that bias can nevertheless improve prediction on new data.

The deliberately introduced bias can improve prediction on new data because it also reduces the variance. The coefficients get shrunk towards zero.

  1. If only a few of many predictors are believed to matter and interpretability is important, which method is the more natural choice? Why?

In this case, the more natural choice is LASSO because it will eliminate the predictors that matter less to the model and create a simpler model that is easy to interpret.

  1. If many highly correlated predictors each carry some signal and you want them to share credit, which method is often preferable? Why?

In this case, ridge is often preferable becaues it forces each predictor to have a coefficient, unlike LASSO, which moves more sharply towards 0 and can force predictors to have coefficients of 0.

  1. Explain why lambda.1se usually produces a simpler model than lambda.min while retaining similar estimated predictive performance.

lambda.1ase usually produces a simpler model than lambda.min because it is more likely to remove predictors with a higher lambda value, but it still lowers coefficients enough to predict well.

Out-of-Sample Model Comparison

13. Compare four candidate models with cross-validation

Compare these four fixed candidate formulas:

  1. the full six-predictor model,
  2. the formula selected by best subsets using AIC,
  3. the formula selected by best subsets using BIC, and
  4. an ordinary lm() using the predictors with nonzero LASSO coefficients at lambda.1se.

Use 5-fold cross-validation repeated 20 times, giving 100 held-out RMSE values for each model. Every fit must use the analysis portion of a split, and every RMSE must use that split’s assessment portion. Report the mean and standard deviation of RMSE for each model, then create side-by-side boxplots of the 100 RMSE values.

When turning a bestglm result into a formula for refitting, build a clean formula from the selected predictor names, for example reformulate(names(coef(best_model))[-1], response = "brozek"). A formula extracted directly from a bestglm fit can retain full-data vectors that do not work inside a resampling fold.

n <- nrow(bodyfat)
rmse_mat <- matrix(NA, nrow = 100, ncol = 4)
colnames(rmse_mat) <- c("full", "aic", "bic", "lasso")

rmse <- function(fit, data) {
  sqrt(mean((predict(fit, data) - data$brozek)^2))
}

row <- 1
for (r in 1:20) {
  folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n))

  for (k in 1:5) {
    test_data  <- bodyfat[folds == k, ]
    train_data <- bodyfat[folds != k, ]

    full_fit  <- lm(brozek ~ ., data = train_data)
    aic_fit   <- lm(brozek ~ height + neck + chest + abdom,
      data = train_data)
    bic_fit   <- lm(brozek ~ weight + abdom, data = train_data)
    lasso_fit <- lm(brozek ~ age + height + neck + abdom,
      data = train_data)

    rmse_mat[row, "full"]  <- rmse(full_fit, test_data)
    rmse_mat[row, "aic"]   <- rmse(aic_fit, test_data)
    rmse_mat[row, "bic"]   <- rmse(bic_fit, test_data)
    rmse_mat[row, "lasso"] <- rmse(lasso_fit, test_data)

    row <- row + 1
  }
}

# Mean RMSE for each model
colMeans(rmse_mat)
    full      aic      bic    lasso 
4.089701 4.069996 4.090949 4.078719 
# Standard deviation of RMSE for each model
apply(rmse_mat, 2, sd)
     full       aic       bic     lasso 
0.3039333 0.2981837 0.2968152 0.3153858 
boxplot(rmse_mat,
  main = "Side-by-side boxplots for RMSE from all samples",
  xlab = "Models",
  ylab = "Sample prediction RMSEs")

14. Interpret the cross-validation evidence

Answer each part using your numerical results and plot.

  1. Which model has the smallest average held-out RMSE?

The model selected by AIC has the smallest average held-out RMSE, at 4.070.

  1. Are the differences in average RMSE large relative to the split-to-split variability? Explain why the smallest displayed average is not automatically a decisive winner.

The differences in average RMSE are not large relative to the split-to-split variability. We can see from the plots that the smallest RMSE for each of the models falls below 3.5, and the largest for each falls above 4.5, a range of more than 1. However, the differences in average RMSE are less than .03, with the smallest being 4.070 and the largest being 4.090. This suggests that on the average, there is not a large difference in the ability of the models to predict, and that we should look at other criteria to decide which model is best.

  1. Why might the full model have the strongest ordinary in-sample R2 but fail to have the best cross-validated RMSE?

The full model might have the strongest ordinary in-sample R2 but fail to have the best cross-validated RMSE because it takes into account every single predicto, which boosts R2, but might not have the best predictive value.

15. Choose a final model

Choose a final subset of predictors. Defend the choice by reconciling predictive performance, model complexity, multicollinearity, and interpretability. More than one conclusion can earn full credit if the evidence is used carefully.

The final subset of predictors I will choose is the subset generated by LASSO: age, height, neck, and, abdomen. While it did have the highest mean RMSE of the four models, it also had the smallest standard deviation, and the spread of both RMSE and standard deviation was extremely narrow. The model is reasonably simple with only four predictors. We will test for multicollinearity, but a gut check says that it is probably not a large problem, with the possible exception of neck and abdomen circumference. It seems unlikely that age and height are related to each other or to the other two predictors, with the caveat that older men tend to get shorter than they were in their prime. The model is also very interpretable and generizable to groups, which is valuable for medical scenarios in which treatments or plans are often recommended based on easy-to-measure characteristics and observed patterns within those characteristics (i.e. “tall older men with neck circumference x and abdomen circumference y tend to have around za to zb% body fat”). (Disclosure: I wrote this before realizing that I had done the cross validation wrong, and would not have chosen this model had I known that the spread was larger.)

bodyfat_final_mod <- lm(brozek ~ age + height + neck + abdom, data = bodyfat)

The residuals vs. fitted plot looks nice, with no curve or trend. The only abnormality is that there are more points on the left side of the graph (with fitted values closer to zero) and a seeming group of outliers scattered on either side of the horizontal line.
The added-variable plots, however, do not look great. They do not seem to be very linear at all, except for abdominal circumference. I’m reconsidering: should I have chosen the model with just weight?

17. Normality of errors

final_with_resids |>
  ggplot(aes(x = residual)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 25, 
    fill = "#d7d1c8", color = "white") +

    args = list(mean = mean(final_with_resids$residual),

  labs(x = "Residual" ,y = "Density", title = "Residual Histogram")
bodyfat_final_mod <- bodyfat |>
  mutate(std_residual = rstandard(bodyfat_final_mod))
ggplot(bodyfat_final_mod, aes(sample = std_residual)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = .6) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "#2f5f8f", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Standardized residual quantiles",
    title = "Normal QQ plot")
shapiro.test(final_with_resids$residual)

    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  final_with_resids$residual
W = 0.99018, p-value = 0.08983

The histogram is rather comical, frankly. While I ordinarily won’t complain about my residuals being too close to the middle (my model being too accurate), the fact of the matter is that they are not spread out enough to fit the normal distribution well, as confirmed by the QQ-plot.
The Shapiro-Wilk test is a little deceptive here, as at a standard significance level, it is insufficient to reject the null hypothesis. It is possible that the p-value is higher than expected because the values are largely contained within the normal distribution, although they may not come from it; there are no extreme residual outliers beyond what is expected.

18. Equal variance

Using the fitted vs. residual plot from above, we can see that perhaps there is a little funnel that opens from right to left. But largely, there are no patterns in the equal variance plot.

Conclusions

21. Overall adequacy

Does your final model adequately satisfy the regression conditions for its intended use? Identify any remaining limitation.

The biggest concern is multicollinearity between neck and abdomen.

22. Communicate the result

In 4-6 sentences, explain your model-building process and final recommendation to a non-statistician. Distinguish clearly between evidence about prediction and evidence about individual predictor effects.

To build the model, we started with all of the factors that were collected by the researchers. We then checked to make sure that we could properly analyze the data before trying to make the model simpler by seeing which predictors we could remove while still predicting accurately. We came to the conclusion that we could safely remove weight and chest circumference from the model because it still predicted body fat percentage reasonably well without those factors.
